claims.claim: The SQL analytics endpoint is read-only for Delta table data. No INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE.
You can create views, functions and stored procedures in the SQL analytics endpoint.
Fabric Warehouse supports explicit multi-table transactions with BEGIN TRAN, COMMIT TRAN and ROLLBACK TRAN.
Metadata sync runs in the background, and you can refresh it from the portal, the REST API or sys.sp_dw_refresh_ext_table.
A warehouse reads lakehouse tables in the same workspace with three-part names, and transactions can span them.
Under normal conditions the lag between a lakehouse and its SQL analytics endpoint is under one minute; the background sync stops after 15 minutes without query activity.

concept_html:
Fabric gives you three ways to hold and query tables. All three store data as Delta tables in OneLake. They differ in who writes the data and in which language.

Lakehouse. You write with Spark: notebooks, Spark job definitions, Dataflows Gen2 or pipelines. It holds files and Delta tables side by side. Choose it for raw files, PySpark transformations and data science. This is the closest match to your Databricks work.

SQL analytics endpoint. Every lakehouse gets one automatically. It gives a read-only T-SQL surface over the lakehouse's Delta tables. You can SELECT, and you can create views, functions and stored procedures. You cannot INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE table data through it. It picks up new or changed tables through a metadata sync. Microsoft documents the usual lag as under one minute, but it varies.

Warehouse. You write with T-SQL. It supports full DML and DDL, and multi-table transactions. Choose it when a team works in T-SQL, loads data with stored procedures, or needs several tables to change together or not at all.

One rule decides most cases: who writes the data, and in which language? Spark writers go to a lakehouse. T-SQL writers go to a warehouse. T-SQL readers of lakehouse data use the SQL analytics endpoint.

You do not have to copy data between them. A warehouse query reads lakehouse tables in the same workspace with a three-part name: lakehouse_name.schema.table. Direct Lake semantic models read from either.

Check the status of each feature you rely on in VERSIONS.md before you build. Fabric changes monthly.

lines: -- Connected to warehouse wh_finance
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.close_month @period CHAR(7) AS
BEGIN
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE dbo.ledger SET status = 'closed' WHERE period = @period;
INSERT INTO dbo.balances (account_id, period, balance)
SELECT account_id, @period, SUM(amount) FROM dbo.ledger
WHERE period = @period GROUP BY account_id;
DELETE FROM dbo.open_items WHERE period = @period;
COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END;

notes.html: The T-SQL writer works in a warehouse, which supports full DML.
All three changes commit together or not at all. Warehouses support multi-table transactions.
Name the target columns. An INSERT without a column list breaks when someone adds a column.

exercises.primer:
`NULLIF(a, b)` returns NULL when `a` equals `b`, and `a` otherwise. Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL, so dividing by `NULLIF(x, 0)` turns a zero divisor into a NULL result instead of an error:

```sql
SELECT 10 / NULLIF(0, 0);   -- NULL
SELECT 10 / NULLIF(5, 0);   -- 2
```

`CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ...` saves a query under a name. Reading the view runs the query.

title: Lakehouse, Warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint
why_html:
A team moves a finance reconciliation from SQL Server to Fabric. They land every table in a lakehouse, because the Databricks team already uses lakehouses. The month-end stored procedure updates three tables. On the SQL analytics endpoint it fails on its first UPDATE, because the endpoint is read-only.

Under deadline, someone rewrites it as three separate Spark notebook writes. On one month-end the second notebook fails. Table one holds the new month and table three holds the old one, and the reconciliation report shows a balance that does not tie. A warehouse transaction would have rolled back all three tables together.
